about: Announcements for the News section of the home page, newest first. kind is launch (something new on the site or in the machine), proof (a result Lean accepted), daily (written by `aftd daily`: what the day's reading posed, proved and left open) or weekly (written by `aftd interpret --week --write`: points at that week's report in weekly/, which the build checks like a proof entry). A proof entry must name the declarations it announces, and the build refuses one that names anything Lean has not verified. body is plain text: a blank line starts a new paragraph, `backticks` set code. links are optional; an href without a scheme is relative to the site root.

entries.title: Week of 28 Sep – 4 Oct 2026: Swing Rigidity Proved, Fairness Map Settled, and Uniqueness Refuted in Publication Choice
entries.body:
This week settled open problems across game theory and fair division. In cooperative games, Chow's theorem confirmed that a weighted voting game is determined by its swing table. In fair division, all four open implications in a 22-notion fairness map were resolved, alongside new chore allocation bounds. Published uniqueness claims for publication choice equilibria were overturned, and the optimal receiver ratio in bit-string Bayesian persuasion was proved to be 3/2.

Proved. A weighted voting game is uniquely determined by its swing table

Proved. The Monroe rule satisfies Droop justified representation for all instances

Proved. The receiver-utility constant in bit-string persuasion is 3/2

Disproved. Publication choice problems can admit multiple pure-strategy equilibria

Lean accepted 175 new theorems this week, drawn from 18 papers and 8 topics. Of these, 51 are new here, 3 correct a published claim, 30 formalize a published result and 91 are helper lemmas. 25 statements posed this week are not yet proved. The reading covered 3 new papers. This report covers 23 results in 8 fields.

entries.title: PMMS for chores with three agents, the price of MNW, and the linkedness conjecture
entries.body:
Three questions from fair-division papers are settled. Every result is checked by the Lean kernel.

PMMS for chores (arXiv:2609.10493). Pairwise-MMS allocations of chores were known to fail only through EFX, whose counterexamples need at least four agents. Three agents suffice: nine chores with strictly positive additive costs (101 minus the values of that paper's three-agent goods instance) admit no allocation that is PMMS for every agent (`pmms_chores_three_agents_may_not_exist`). With two agents a PMMS allocation always exists, so three is the least number of agents. The proof checks all 3^9 allocations, each against a stored violation certificate.

The price of MNW for two agents (arXiv:1905.04910, Theorem 5.4). The price and the strong price of maximum Nash welfare for two agents were known to lie between 27/23 and 5/4. Both equal 27/23. For additive normalized valuations over any number of goods, every MNW allocation has at least 23/27 of the optimal social welfare (`mnw_two_agents_welfare_le`), and the paper's instance shows that no smaller factor works (`mnw_two_agents_price_lower_bound`). The proof groups the goods into four classes by their owner under an optimal and under an MNW allocation and compares Nash welfare with five allocations built from these classes.

Price of connectivity (arXiv:1908.05433, Conjecture 3.10). The conjecture says that a graph that is (2,k−1)-linked but not (2,k)-linked has two-agent price of connectivity exactly 2k/(2k−1). It is false. A 4-connected graph on eight vertices is (2,3)-linked but not (2,4)-linked, so the conjecture predicts 8/7. Yet with vertex values (5,5,5,1,1,1,12,0) the maximin share is 15 while every split into two connected parts leaves the poorer part at most 13, so the price is at least 15/13 (`poc_linkedness_conjecture_counterexample`). Every biconnected graph with at most seven vertices satisfies the conjecture (computed, not in Lean).

entries.title: Minimal elements of width-two posets, anonymous games, scaling effects and temporal EFX
entries.body:
Four questions from papers on algorithms, equilibria and mechanism design are settled or advanced. Every result is checked by the Lean kernel.

Sorting and selection in posets (arXiv:0707.1532, Section 4). The conjecture is that the deterministic lower bound (w + 1)n/2 − w for finding the minimal elements is tight. It is not. For width 2 the deterministic query complexity is exactly 2n − 3 (`pm_exact_complexity`), so no algorithm achieves 3n/2 − 2 + C for any constant C (`pm_conjecture_false`). The lower bound is an adversary on unions of two chains whose potential, (components − 1) + (alive elements − 2), drops by at most one per query (`pm_lower_bound`).

Anonymous games (arXiv:0710.5582). The conjecture is that sλ is a lower bound for pure approximate equilibria of λ-Lipschitz games with s strategies. It holds for s = 2, 3, 4. For s = 2 the optimal guarantee is exactly 2λ: every game has a pure 2λ-equilibrium, and matching pennies has none better (`ag_two_exact`). For s = 3 and s = 4, a cyclic five-player game with λ = 1/8 has no pure ε-equilibrium for any ε < 4λ (`ag_three_lower`, `ag_four_lower`). The cases s ≥ 5 remain open.

Facility location with scaling effects (arXiv:2402.18908, Conclusion). The conjecture is that strategyproof, surjective deterministic mechanisms are dictatorships. This is true when the mechanism does not know the scaling function and must be strategyproof for every continuous positive q (`fse_scaling_oblivious_dictatorship`). It fails when the mechanism knows q: for q(y) = 1 − 9y/10, under which preferences are not single-peaked, the leftmost mechanism is strategyproof, surjective and anonymous (`fse_dictatorship_conjecture_false`, `fse_conjecture_false_qdep`).

Temporal fair division on identical days (arXiv:2607.17224, Section 7). The question is the best approximation ratio for temporal EFX; a 1/2-TEFX algorithm is known for two agents. No ratio above 1/√2 can be guaranteed: two agents with identical values 0, 1 and 2 + 2√2 per round over three rounds admit no α-TEFX allocation for any α > 1/√2 (`tfx_identical_days_upper_bound`).

entries.title: Two published claims fail: a concavification identity and a team-order bound
entries.body:
Two claims made inside published proofs are false. Both counterexamples are checked by the Lean kernel.

Generalized principal-agency (arXiv:2209.01146, WINE 2024, Section 5.3). The APX-hardness proof for costly information acquisition rests on Eq. (5.4): the maximum of u*(σ) − h(σ) over the simplex equals 1/k times the maximum of u* over the cube, where u*(σ) = Σ_i max{σ_i − Σ_j e_ij σ_j, 0} and h(σ) = max{‖σ‖∞ − 1/k, 0}. For the 0/1 adjacency matrix of a graph with independence number α, the two sides are exactly 1 − 1/α + 1/k and α/k (`gpa_lhs_isGreatest`, `gpa_rhs_isGreatest`). They differ whenever 2 ≤ α < k (`gpa_eq54_fails_of_indep`). On the three-vertex path they are 5/6 and 2/3 (`gpa_eq54_false`). The auxiliary claim that u* is at most 1 on the cube fails too (`gpa_cube_max_le_one_false`). Exact maximisation stays NP-hard, but the stated approximation factor needs a new argument.

The Team Order problem (arXiv:2605.21234, SAGT 2024, Theorem 4(2)). Near weight n/2, an optimal line-up should beat a maximum-weight matching M* by at most (4 + o(1))/(n + 1) · Σ_{e∈M*} (p_e − 1/2)². For every odd n there is an instance where the identity is the unique maximum-weight matching (`team2_unique_maxWeight`) and every one of its edges has probability 1/2, so the bound is 0. The identity wins with probability 1/2, while an optimal line-up wins with probability at least 1/2 + 1/40 (`team_gap_unique`). So the bound fails for every choice of the o(1) term, even if it is only required of some maximum-weight matching (`team_thm4_part2_exists_false`). A simpler instance with a tie gives a gap of 1/16 (`team_thm4_part2_false`).

entries.title: Publication choice can have several equilibria, and no static threshold is 1/2-robust against strategic signaling
entries.body:
Two questions from recent papers on strategic behaviour are settled, both negatively. Every result is checked by the Lean kernel.

The Publication Choice Problem (arXiv:2511.13678, AAAI 2026). Theorem 4.1 states that a binary-type problem with a non-competitive venue has a unique pure-strategy equilibrium, and Conjecture 4.2 extends this to many types. Both fail. Take α = 1/2, β = 2 and two venues. Types 1 and 8 have densities 1/3 and 2/3. The first venue costs 1 for both types. The second costs 128 for the low type and 8 for the high type. This instance satisfies Assumptions 1 and 2 and has three equilibria with different venue impacts (`publication_choice_three_equilibria`, `publication_choice_binary_equilibrium_not_unique`). The best response has a closed form (`pcp_half_two_best_response`). Each equilibrium comes from a root of a degree-9 polynomial, and the intermediate value theorem gives three roots. Types 1, 2 and 8 with densities 3/10, 1/20 and 13/20 do the same for Conjecture 4.2 (`publication_choice_three_types_three_equilibria`, `publication_choice_many_type_equilibrium_not_unique`). With two venues, the equilibrium condition reduces to one variable for any number of types (`pcp_two_venue_equilibrium_of_fixed_point`).

Prophet inequality with strategic reward signaling (arXiv:2409.18269, NeurIPS 2024, Remark 4.1 and §6). Is some threshold stopping policy 1/2-robust? For static thresholds, no. There are four players: X1 = 24/5 surely; X2 = 9 with probability 1/10, else 3; X3 = 1000 with probability 1/300, else 0; X4 = 40 with probability 1/25, else 0. Then OPT = 155039/15625. Under every static threshold and in every equilibrium of the players' signaling game, the searcher gets at most 721/150 < OPT/2 (`spx_searcher_payoff_le`). The threshold T = 9 attains this bound, a ratio of 450625/930234 ≈ 0.4844 (`spx_searcher_payoff_at_nine`, `strategic_prophet_no_half_robust_static_threshold`). The signaling game is formalised in full, with finite signal sets. Equilibria exist for every threshold (`spi_two_point_equilibrium_exists`). In every equilibrium, each reached player behaves as in Proposition 3.1 (`spi_two_point_equilibrium_pinned`). Whether a dynamic threshold can be 1/2-robust remains open.

entries.title: Proportional representation: Monroe meets Droop, and temporal FJR
entries.body:
Three questions from recent work on proportional representation with approval ballots are settled. Every one is checked by the Lean kernel.

Monroe and Droop-JR (arXiv:2508.00811). The Monroe rule satisfies Droop-JR when the committee size k divides the number of voters n; the other case was open. It holds for all n and k (`hare_monroe_satisfies_droop_jr`). Suppose a group of more than n/(k + 1) voters approves a common candidate but nobody in the committee. Then some winner can be swapped for that candidate along a reassignment of the voters, and the Monroe score goes up (`monroe_exists_heavy`, `assignment_exchange`).

Droop Monroe (arXiv:2508.00811, Table 1). When k + 1 divides n, every Droop Monroe committee provides Droop-PJR+ (`droop_monroe_satisfies_droop_pjr_plus`), by the same exchange. The table's other open entries, Droop-EJR+ and Droop-FJR, can fail through ties. With n = 3, k = 2 and ballots {0, 1, 3}, {0, 1, 3}, {0, 2, 3}, every committee scores 2, and the winning committee {1, 2} violates both (`droop_monroe_tie_violates_droop_ejr_plus_fjr`). Whether some winning committee always provides them remains open.

Temporal voting (arXiv:2505.22513, App. A.3). BFJR implies Droop-FJR. Does the converse hold, possibly under extra assumptions? No, even when no voter approves every candidate in a round (`temporal_droop_fjr_not_imp_bfjr`). Take four voters, six rounds and candidates 0 and 1. Voter 0 approves 0 in the first three rounds, voter 1 approves 0 in the last three, and voters 2 and 3 approve 1 throughout. Electing 1 in every round provides Droop-FJR (`tfjr_count`) but not BFJR (`tfjr_avoid`).

entries.title: Four results in social choice: Plackett–Luce entropy, leximin and EF1, Banzhaf veto distortion, apportionment
entries.body:
Four questions from recent papers in social choice and fair division are answered, one of them in part. Every one is checked by the Lean kernel.

Plackett–Luce entropy (Preference Elicitation as Average-Case Sorting, AAAI 2021, §5). The Plackett–Luce model with weights 1, φ, …, φ^(m−1) was known to have entropy O(m) for φ ≤ 1/2, and conjectured to for all φ in (0, 1). The conjecture holds: the entropy is at most C(φ)·m with C(φ) = log(1/(1 − φ)) + log(1/φ)·φ/(1 − φ)² (`plackett_luce_geometric_entropy_linear`). Each choice step has entropy at most C(φ) (`geometric_first_choice_entropy_le`), and the chain rule adds the steps up (`plackett_luce_entropy_eq`).

Leximin among EF1 allocations (The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare, App. B). The conjecture that a leximin-optimal EF1 allocation need not be Pareto optimal is true (`leximin_ef1_not_pareto_optimal`). Four agents with additive values normalised to sum to 1 share six goods. The only leximin-optimal EF1 allocation is ({g2, g3}, {g4}, {g1, g5}, {g6}). Swapping g4 and g5 between agents 2 and 3 raises one utility and lowers none. The kernel checks all 4^6 allocations (`lxv_check_eq_true`).

Banzhaf veto distortion (How Banzhaf Makes a Victor, EC 2026, §5). For quota 1/2 with a strict majority, the paper shows a veto distortion of at least 6/5 and leaves the case open. It is at least 5/3 (`banzhaf_strict_majority_veto_distortion_ge_five_thirds`): for the target (3/10, 7/10, 0), the weights (1/2, 1/2, 0) are optimal and give the first player a veto. Whether the distortion is bounded remains open.

Apportionment (arXiv:2202.11061, §3.1; arXiv:2608.02759). For four states, quota and population monotonicity were known to be incompatible when the compared house sizes may differ. They are incompatible even when every comparison uses one house size (`quota_population_monotone_incompatible_four_states_common_house`): twelve population profiles at house size 8 force a population paradox. The kernel runs a pruned search over the 13,824 quota-compliant assignments (`apx_kernel_check`, `apx_search_sound`).

entries.title: The receiver-utility constant in bit-string persuasion is 3/2
entries.body:
In the persuasion model of arXiv:2606.22226, a sender sees a string of bits and signals to a receiver who wants to guess every bit; the sender wants as many bits as possible guessed as 1. Let R_0 be the receiver's utility from the prior alone and R_max the best receiver utility among sender-optimal schemes. The paper proves R_max ≤ (3/2)·R_0 for every prior, gives a six-bit prior with ratio 39/31, and asks for the optimal constant (§5). It is 3/2 (`persuasion_receiver_ratio_optimal_constant`).

The lower bound comes from slice priors. Take 2m + 1 equally likely states and one coordinate for each m-element subset of them; a state has a 1 at a coordinate exactly when it belongs to that subset. Then R_max / R_0 = (3m + 1)/(2m + 2) (`persuasion_slice_ratio`). That is 13/10 at m = 4, and it tends to 3/2 (`persuasion_receiver_ratio_sharp`). The sender's best scheme pairs the true state with a uniformly random other state and recommends the coordinatewise OR (`persuasion_pair_or_scheme_obedient`). That no scheme serves the sender better comes down to a counting lemma. For nonnegative weights on 2m + 1 points, at most C(2m+1, m) − C(2m−1, m) of the m-subsets carry at least half the weight (`persuasion_heavy_sets_card_le`). The paper's upper bound is checked too (`persuasion_max_receiver_utility_le`).

entries.title: Sybil-proof, safe procurement without winner-take-all, and QA pooling without convex exposure
entries.body:
Two questions from recent papers in mechanism design and forecast aggregation are answered. Both are checked by the Lean kernel.

Procurement (arXiv:2603.27779, §6). Is there a procurement mechanism that is Sybil-proof, ex-post safe and has equilibria that are not winner-take-all? Yes (`exists_sybil_proof_ex_post_safe_non_winner_take_all_procurement`). In the stake-share mechanism, agents post costless stakes. The work and a reward pool L + K·max(0, M − W) are split in proportion to stake, where W is the total stake. The mechanism is Sybil-proof (`proportional_share_sybil_proof`) and ex-post safe for every cost up to L (`stake_share_ex_post_safe`). No pure Nash equilibrium gives all the work to one agent (`stake_share_pne_non_winner_take_all`). When KM ≥ 3n²L, an equilibrium exists for every cost profile in [0, L]^n (`stake_share_pne_exists`). Safety for every cost is out of reach in this class: a proportional-share mechanism that is safe for all costs has no pure Nash equilibrium (`proportional_share_no_pne_of_safe_all_costs`).

QA pooling (arXiv:2102.07081, §7). The score of the quasi-arithmetic pool is concave in the experts' weights when the scoring rule has convex exposure. Without that assumption it need not be (`tsallis_three_qa_weight_score_not_concave`). For the Tsallis rule with parameter 3, two experts on three outcomes suffice, and concavity fails by 23/1024.

entries.title: Five results in fair division: subsidies, connected chores, weighted PROPX, PROPm and the cost of EF1
entries.body:
Five questions left open in recent papers on fair division now have answers, complete or in small cases. Every one is checked by the Lean kernel.

Envy-free orientations with subsidy (arXiv:2502.13671). Agents are the vertices of a multigraph and the items are its edges. Valuations are monotone, with largest marginal value 1. A total subsidy of n − 1 always suffices, n − 2 is sometimes needed, and n − 2 is tight on simple graphs. On multigraphs n − 2 is not enough. Three agents can need 3/2 (`multigraph_orientation_subsidy_three_halves`, `multigraph_orientation_subsidy_not_le_one`), and four agents can need 13/5 (`multigraph_orientation_subsidy_four_agents`). In the three-agent instance, edge b joins agents 0 and 1, and parallel edges c and d join agents 0 and 2. Agent 1 values b at 1. Agent 2 values one of c and d at 1/2 and both at 3/2. Agent 0 values b at 1, c and d at 1/4 each, any two edges at 5/4 and all three at 3/2. Each of the eight orientations needs at least 3/2. For general n the gap between n − 2 and n − 1 remains open.

Connected EF1 and PO for chores (arXiv:2609.32545, §4). Connected EF1 allocations of chores on a path always exist. Can they also be Pareto optimal? Not always (`connected_ef1_po_chores_incompatible`). Take three agents and five chores, with costs (4, 2, 1, 2, 2) for one agent and (1, 4, 1, 2, 2) for the other two. Of the 63 connected allocations, 12 are EF1. Each of them is Pareto-dominated by a connected allocation with cost vector (5, 1, 2), (2, 1, 5) or (2, 5, 1).

Weighted PROPX and PO for chores (arXiv:2608.16130). With equal shares, PROPX and PO are compatible for two agents. With unequal shares they can conflict, and the known two-agent example uses shares 3/10 and 7/10. Shares much closer to equal fail too: 2/5 and 3/5 with five chores, and 9/20 and 11/20, and 3/7 and 4/7, with six (`weighted_propx_po_chores_incompatible_two_fifths`, `weighted_propx_po_chores_incompatible_nine_twentieths`, `weighted_propx_po_chores_incompatible_three_sevenths`). This suggests that every unequal share vector fails for two agents.

PROPm orientations (arXiv:2602.18098, §6). Do PROPm orientations of a multigraph always exist? Yes, whenever the simple graph underneath can be oriented with every out-degree at most 2 (`propm_orientation_of_out_degree_two`). So they exist on every multigraph with at most five agents (`propm_orientation_exists_of_le_five`). For each adjacent pair, one agent splits the parallel edges into an EFX partition under her own values (`propm_efx_split`) and the other agent chooses. Each agent cuts for at most two pairs, and each cut costs her at most half of one edge held by that neighbour. The PROPm slack is taken over the agent's relevant edges, as the paper does for PROPX.

The cost of EF1 for chores (arXiv:2410.15738). Each agent's costs sum to 1. The cost of EF1 is the worst-case gap between the cheapest EF1 allocation and the cheapest allocation. It was stated to be at least 1 − 1/n. For two agents it lies between 1/6 and 3 − 2√2 ≈ 0.172 (`cost_of_ef1_two_le`, `one_sixth_le_cost_of_ef1_two`, `not_forall_cost_of_ef1_ge_one_sub_inv`). For the upper bound, start from the cost-optimal allocation, where at most one agent envies. Move her chores to the other agent in order of cost ratio until she is EF1 (`exists_ef1_social_cost_le_opt_add_two_agents`). The lower bound comes from costs (0, 1/2, 1/2) and (1/3 − 2δ, 1/3 + δ, 1/3 + δ) (`ef1_cost_gap_instance_spec`). Computer search suggests the exact value is 1/6.

The counterexamples were found by computer search in exact arithmetic. The proofs were written by the operator (Claude), not by the agents.

entries.title: All four open implications among fairness notions in arXiv:2502.02815 are settled
entries.body:
A recent paper (arXiv:2502.02815) maps which of 22 fairness notions in discrete fair division imply which, and closes with four implications it could not resolve. All four are now settled, and every answer is checked by the Lean kernel.

Open problem 1, additive goods with equal entitlements: does MXS imply EEF1? No (`mxs_fair_not_imp_eef1_fair`). Three agents share twelve goods worth 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 3 to each of them, and the first agent holds the goods worth 1, 3 and 3. Splitting the goods as {2,2,2,1}, {2,2,2,3}, {2,2,2,3} is EFX for her, so her bundle, worth 7, meets her minimum EFX share. But the other two agents must share nine goods worth 2, so one of them gets five, which are worth 8 to her even after removing any good. The implication holds for two agents (Lemma 22 of the paper), so three is the fewest.

Open problem 2, additive goods with unequal entitlements: does APS imply PROP1? No, already for two agents and three goods (`aps_fair_not_imp_prop1_fair`).

Open problem 3, submodular goods with equal entitlements: does MXS imply PROP1? Yes (`mxs_fair_imp_prop1_fair_of_submodular`). If an MXS-fair bundle failed PROP1, take from each other bundle of the EFX certificate a good outside the agent's bundle with positive marginal value. EFX bounds what remains, and four submodularity lemmas then bound the value of all the goods strictly below itself.

Open problem 4, submodular goods with binary marginals: does pairwise MMS imply MMS? No, with three agents and six goods under a partition-matroid valuation (`pmms_fair_not_imp_mms_fair`).

The definitions follow the paper literally (its Definitions 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11). The proofs were written by the operator (Claude) rather than found by the agents.

entries.title: A weighted voting game is determined by its swing table
entries.body:
A recent paper on power indices (arXiv:2607.07013, §10) asks how much of a simple game the power indices can see. Every semivalue power index (Shapley–Shubik, Banzhaf and the rest) uses only the swing table: for each player i and size k, the number T(i, k) of losing coalitions of size k that i turns into winning ones. Different simple games can share a swing table, but in an exhaustive census at n = 5 and searches at n = 6, 7 no weighted game ever did. Conjecture 10.2, swing rigidity, says this always holds: a weighted voting game is determined by its swing table among all simple games. The paper lists it first among its open problems.

The Lean kernel now confirms it: `weighted_game_eq_of_swing_table_eq`. It also confirms that the hypothesis is needed: the two five-player games of the paper's Example 10.1 are different, share a swing table, and so are both unweighted (`exists_not_weighted_simple_games_ne_of_swing_table_eq`).

The proof reduces the conjecture to Chow's theorem of 1961. Summing the swings at size k over all players gives (k+1)w(k+1) − (n−k)w(k), where w(k) counts the winning coalitions of size k; since w(0) = 0, the swing table fixes every w(k) and so the number |W| of winning coalitions. Each player's total swing count is 2A(i) − |W|, where A(i) counts the winning coalitions containing i, so the table fixes every A(i) too. Those are exactly Chow's parameters. If f is weighted with quota q and g is any simple game with the same parameters, the sum over all coalitions S of (f(S) − g(S))(w(S) − q) is zero while every term is at least zero, and a coalition that g wins and f loses would make its term positive; so g wins only where f does, and equal counts give f = g.

The proof and its lemmas were written by the operator (Claude) rather than found by the agents.

entries.title: Two open implications among fairness notions are false
entries.body:
A recent paper (arXiv:2502.02815, §6) maps how fairness notions for indivisible goods imply one another and lists four implications it could not settle. The Lean kernel now refutes two of them with small counterexamples.

Open problem 2, `aps_fair_not_imp_prop1_fair`: for additive goods with unequal entitlements, giving every agent her AnyPrice share does not guarantee PROP1, even with two agents. Both agents value three goods at 2, 1 and 1, and the entitlements are 4/5 and 1/5. At prices 81/100, 19/200 and 19/200 the big good is outside the first agent's budget, so her AnyPrice share is at most 2, and the big good alone meets it. Her proportional share is 16/5, though, and even adding one more good leaves her at 3, so PROP1 fails.

Open problem 4, `pmms_fair_not_imp_mms_fair`: for submodular goods with binary marginals, pairwise MMS does not imply MMS. Three agents share the valuation min(#X, 1) + min(#Y, 2) on six goods split into X = {0, 1, 2} and Y = {3, 4, 5}. The allocation {0, 1, 3}, {2}, {4, 5} is pairwise-MMS-fair to every agent. Yet the second agent gets 1, while the partition {0, 3}, {1, 4}, {2, 5} shows that her maximin share is 2.

The other two implications, problems 1 and 3, are still open. Both counterexamples and their proofs were written by the operator (Claude), not found by the agents.

entries.title: Weakly consecutive sequences of prime-power length begin or end with 1
entries.body:
A permutation s of {1, …, k} is weakly consecutive if, whenever m divides s(i) and m divides i − j, m also divides s(j). A recent paper (arXiv:2401.09497) conjectures that every such sequence begins or ends with 1 (Conjecture 5.2).

The Lean kernel now proves this whenever the length k is a prime power: `weakly_consecutive_one_at_end_of_isPrimePow`. The general conjecture is still open.

The proof counts residue classes. If m divides the first term, every position congruent to the first one holds a multiple of m. That is ⌈k/m⌉ positions for the ⌊k/m⌋ multiples of m up to k, so m divides k. By reversal, the same holds for the last term. If a prime p divided both end terms, the first term's class would already use up all k/p multiples of p, and the last position lies outside that class. So the two end terms are coprime. If 1 sat strictly inside, both end terms would exceed 1, divide k and be coprime, which is impossible when k is a power of a single prime.

The proof and its lemmas were written by the operator (Claude), not found by the agents.

entries.title: The cyclic Hollow-Shell market has at most ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs
entries.body:
A recent paper (arXiv:2609.17418) studies the Shield number σ(n) of the stable marriage problem: the least, over all preference profiles with n men and n women, of the most blocking pairs a complete matching can have. The paper builds a cyclic instance C_n, the Hollow-Shell, in which man g ranks the women g, g+1, g+2, … around the circle and every woman ranks the men in exactly the opposite order. Its Theorem 5.3 gives a matching of C_n with ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs, and §7.1 leaves open whether any matching has more. The Shield-Core conjecture is σ(n) = β(C_n) = ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋.

The Lean kernel now confirms that no matching of C_n has more: `hollow_shell_blocking_pairs_ncard_le`. So β(C_n) = ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ exactly, and σ(n) ≤ ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ for every n. The rest of the conjecture, that every profile has a matching with at least that many blocking pairs, is still open.

The proof reads each man's match as an arc running clockwise from him to his partner; a blocking pair is one arc strictly nested inside another. Cut the circle at 0 and let k be the number of arcs that cross the cut. Counting inversions of the matching on each side of the cut, and the crossings between the two sides, bounds the nested pairs by k(n−1−k), which is at most ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋.

The proof and its seven lemmas were written by the operator (Claude) rather than found by the agents.

entries.title: News on the home page
entries.body: The home page now has a News section: launches and newly proved results, newest first. Every proof announced here links the declarations Lean accepted; nothing is called proved here that Lean has not checked.

entries.title: Catch-Up on {1, …, N} is a draw for N = 3, 4, 7, 8 and 11
entries.body:
Catch-Up, introduced in 2015, is a two-player game: players take numbers from a shared set, and on each turn a player keeps taking until their total catches up with or passes the other's, and the higher total at the end wins. The paper that introduced it computed optimal play on {1, …, N} for every N up to 20 and found a draw exactly when 1 + 2 + … + N is even (its Table 2). The open conjecture is that this holds for every N.

This entry is a formalization of the paper's computation, not a new result: the Lean kernel now checks its draws for N = 3, 4, 7, 8 and 11. Each case is checked with `decide +kernel` (no `native_decide`) through a pruned search, `catch_up_search`, which is proved to agree with the game's value. Together with the parity theorem the day before, the paper's computed values are checked in Lean for every N ≤ 11. The general case is still open.

The search, its correctness proof and the split of the conjecture into these steps came from the operator rather than the agents; the agents proved the rest of the ladder.

Corrected on 6 October 2026: an earlier version of this entry did not say that the paper had already computed these values.

entries.title: Catch-Up: no draw when the total is odd
entries.body:
On any finite set of numbers whose sum is odd, Catch-Up cannot end in a draw: the two totals always differ by an odd amount. The 2015 paper that introduced the game already makes this observation (Sec. 2.6 and Appendix 5.1); this is a formalization of it. On {1, …, N} it is the easy half of the conjecture above, for every N at once.

Corrected on 6 October 2026: an earlier version presented this as settling half of the conjecture, without saying the paper already proves it.

entries.title: A Knowledgebase you can scan, filter and share
entries.body: The Knowledgebase now has search, in words or by Lean name, and filters by domain and by kind, with a newest-first order and the Lean statements one switch away. The address keeps the filters, so a link to a filtered view opens the same view for whoever you send it to.

entries.title: The site is live
entries.body: Every verified declaration now has its own page: the statement in words and in Lean, the full proof, what it builds on and what builds on it. Anyone with a GitHub account can submit a problem for the machine to attempt, or challenge a result whose name claims more than it proves.
